match.reason: No bank point teaches narratives as a way to show and shape personal and shared identity, or how writers, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander writers, choose to represent their own experiences; the closest, Narratives across cultures and time, only mentions identity in passing at Year 11 depth, and Counter-narratives is related but a different idea.

rejected.title: Narrative and identity
card: Identity is how a person or group understands who they are. It can be personal, such as a person's sense of self, or shared, such as belonging to a family, community or culture.
Narratives can show identity, through a character's choices, language, family and place. They can also shape it, by giving readers ways to see themselves and others.
Writers choose how to represent their own experiences. Writers from different cultures may choose different stories, voices and settings.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander writers may represent their own cultures, Country and histories in their own voices. This is a choice made by each writer, and no single story speaks for everyone.
rejected.remember: Stories can show and shape who people are, and writers choose how to represent their own experiences.

a.q: A novel follows a teenager who moves from Vietnam to Sydney and keeps her family's cooking traditions. How does the narrative show identity?
opts: Her choices and traditions show where she belongs
It lists facts about Sydney's suburbs
It proves all migrants share one identity
It avoids showing her family at all
a.why: The character's choices and traditions show her personal and cultural identity. The story does not claim that all migrants share one identity, because writers represent particular experiences.
a.clue: Look at what the character does and keeps.

b.q: An Aboriginal author writes a memoir about growing up on her grandmother's Country. Which statement about her writing is best?
opts: She chooses how to represent her own experience
She speaks for every Aboriginal person
She must follow the same style as other writers
She cannot show personal identity in a memoir
b.why: A memoir lets the author choose which experiences, voice and setting to present. It does not speak for every Aboriginal person, because each writer represents their own experience and cultures differ.
b.clue: Who decides how the story is told?

version.title: Narrative and identity
card: Identity is how a person or group understands who they are. It can be personal, such as one person's sense of self, or shared, such as belonging to a family, community or culture.
Narratives show identity through a character's choices, language, relationships and places. They can also shape it, by giving readers new ways to see themselves and others.
Writers choose how to represent their own experiences: which events to tell, whose voice to use and what to leave out. These choices shape how readers see a person or a group.
Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander writers tell their own stories in their own voices, after a long history of others writing about them. No single story speaks for every community.
version.remember: Stories show and shape who people are, and writers choose how their own experiences are told.

a.q: In a novel, a girl who moved from Lebanon to Sydney speaks Arabic at home and English at school, and feels part of both. How does the narrative show her identity?
opts: Through her language choices and sense of belonging
Through a list of facts about life in modern Sydney
Through a claim that all migrants feel the same way
Through the setting alone, without her own choices
a.why: Her switching between languages and her sense of belonging to both places show who she is. The novel tells one girl's story, so it does not claim that all migrants feel the same.
a.clue: Look at what she does and how she feels.

b.q: An Aboriginal author writes a memoir, in her own words, about growing up on her grandmother's Country. Why does this matter for identity?
opts: She decides how her own life and culture are shown
She shows the experience of every Aboriginal person
She lets others decide how her community is described
She keeps her identity out of the story she tells
b.why: Telling her own story lets her choose which experiences, voice and places to show, so she shapes how her identity is seen. It is her experience, so it does not speak for every Aboriginal person.
b.clue: Who controls how the story is told?
